bodyText:
What is a Computer?

A computer is an electronic device that accepts data as input, processes it according to a set of instructions, and produces meaningful information as output. The word computer comes from the Latin word computare, meaning to calculate. Modern computers work on the IPO cycle: Input, Processing and Output, with storage supporting each stage.

Data refers to raw, unorganised facts and figures, while information is processed data that is meaningful and useful for decision-making. A computer system consists of hardware, software, data and users. Hardware is the physical part of the computer, software is the set of programs and instructions, and the user is the person who operates the system.

Early Calculating Devices

The history of computers begins with simple counting tools. The abacus, used in ancient China, is considered one of the earliest calculating devices. In 1642, Blaise Pascal invented the Pascaline, a mechanical calculator that could add and subtract. Later, Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz improved mechanical calculation with a machine that could also multiply and divide.

In 1801, Joseph-Marie Jacquard introduced punched cards to control weaving looms. This idea of storing instructions on punched cards later influenced early computer design. In 1890, Herman Hollerith developed a tabulating machine that used punched cards to process data for the United States census, greatly reducing the time needed to count the population.

Charles Babbage and Ada Lovelace

Charles Babbage is known as the Father of the Computer. He designed the Difference Engine in 1822 for automatic calculation of mathematical tables, and then the Analytical Engine in 1837. The Analytical Engine had the essential parts of a modern computer: an input unit, a store (memory), a mill (processor) and an output unit. Although it was never fully built in his lifetime, its design laid the foundation of the modern computer.

Ada Lovelace worked on the Analytical Engine and wrote notes explaining how it could be programmed. She is recognised as the first computer programmer because she described an algorithm intended to be processed by a machine.

From Electromechanical to Electronic Computers

In 1936, Alan Turing proposed the concept of a universal machine, which became the theoretical basis of modern computing. In 1944, Howard Aiken completed the Harvard Mark I, an electromechanical computer. ENIAC, completed in 1945, was one of the first general-purpose electronic computers. It used vacuum tubes and was very large, heavy and power-hungry.

UNIVAC I, delivered in 1951, was the first commercial computer produced in the United States. The invention of the transistor in 1947 and later the integrated circuit made computers smaller, faster, cheaper and more reliable, opening the way to personal computing and the modern digital age.

bodyText:
What is Meant by a Computer Generation?

A generation of computers refers to a stage in the development of computer technology, marked mainly by a change in the electronic component used for processing. Each generation brought computers that were smaller, faster, cheaper and more reliable than those before it. Examiners commonly ask candidates to match a generation with its technology, period and example.

First Generation (1940s to 1950s)

First-generation computers used vacuum tubes for circuitry and magnetic drums for memory. They were very large, consumed a great deal of electricity, produced much heat, and were expensive to operate. Programming was done in machine language, using only binary digits. Examples include ENIAC, EDVAC and UNIVAC I.

Second Generation (1950s to 1960s)

Second-generation computers used transistors instead of vacuum tubes. Transistors were smaller, faster, cheaper and more reliable, and they produced less heat. Assembly language replaced machine language for much programming work, and high-level languages such as FORTRAN and COBOL began to appear. Examples include IBM 1401 and IBM 7090.

Third Generation (1960s to 1970s)

Third-generation computers used integrated circuits (ICs), in which many transistors were placed on a single silicon chip. This made computers smaller, faster and more reliable, and reduced their cost. Keyboards and monitors became common for input and output, and operating systems allowed several programs to run more efficiently. Examples include IBM 360 and IBM 370 series.

Fourth Generation (1970s to Present)

Fourth-generation computers are based on the microprocessor, a complete central processing unit on a single chip. Very Large Scale Integration (VLSI) placed thousands of transistors on one chip, later followed by Ultra Large Scale Integration (ULSI). This generation brought personal computers, graphical user interfaces, computer networks and the internet into everyday life.

Fifth Generation (Present and Future)

Fifth-generation computers are based on artificial intelligence (AI). The aim is to develop machines that can understand natural language, recognise speech and images, learn from experience and make decisions. Technologies associated with this generation include parallel processing, robotics, expert systems and natural language processing.

bodyText:
Classification by Working Principle

Computers can be classified according to how they process data. The three main types are analog computers, digital computers and hybrid computers. The distinction depends on whether data is represented by continuously varying physical quantities, by discrete digits, or by a combination of both.

Analog Computers

An analog computer works with continuous data, such as temperature, pressure, voltage or speed, which change smoothly over time. It measures physical quantities rather than counting digits, and its results are usually approximate rather than exact. Analog computers are fast at certain specialised calculations but are less accurate and less flexible than digital computers.

Common examples include the traditional mercury thermometer, the speedometer of a vehicle, and the slide rule. Analog computers were widely used in engineering and scientific work before digital computers became dominant.

Digital Computers

A digital computer works with discrete data represented in binary form, using the digits 0 and 1. It counts and calculates in exact steps, which makes its results highly accurate. Digital computers are programmable, versatile and able to store large amounts of data, which is why they dominate modern computing.

Examples include desktop computers, laptops, tablets, smartphones and servers. Almost all computers in everyday use today are digital computers.

Hybrid Computers

A hybrid computer combines the features of both analog and digital computers. It accepts analog signals, converts them into digital form for accurate processing and storage, and may convert the results back into analog form for output. This combination makes hybrid computers useful where real-world measurements must be processed with digital precision.

Hybrid computers are used in hospitals, for example in intensive-care monitoring systems, in weather forecasting, and in industrial process control, such as monitoring and controlling machinery in a factory or a petrol station system that measures fuel flow and calculates the digital bill.

bodyText:
Characteristics of Computers

Computers are widely used because they possess a set of strengths that human workers cannot match at the same scale. The most important characteristics are speed, accuracy, diligence, versatility, storage capacity, automation and reliability.

  • Speed: A computer can perform millions of instructions per second, completing in seconds work that would take a human hours or days.

  • Accuracy: A computer produces correct results when it is given correct data and correct instructions. Errors in computer output usually come from faulty input or programming, not from the machine itself.

  • Diligence: Unlike humans, a computer does not get tired, bored or lose concentration. It can repeat the same task millions of times with the same care.

  • Versatility: The same computer can be used for many different tasks, such as writing documents, playing music, browsing the internet and controlling machinery, simply by changing the software.

  • Storage capacity: A computer can store vast amounts of data and retrieve it quickly and accurately when needed.

  • Automation: Once instructions are given, a computer can carry out a sequence of operations automatically, without continuous human intervention.

Limitations of Computers

Despite their power, computers have clear limitations, and examiners often ask candidates to distinguish these from their characteristics.

  • No intelligence of its own: A computer has no intelligence, common sense or judgement. It only follows the instructions given to it and cannot decide what is right or wrong on its own.

  • No feelings or emotions: A computer cannot feel, think creatively in the human sense, or understand emotions.

  • Dependence on instructions: A computer cannot work without a program. If no instructions are provided, it cannot perform any task.

  • Garbage In, Garbage Out (GIGO): If incorrect data or instructions are supplied, the computer will produce incorrect output, however fast or carefully it works.

  • No learning from experience by itself: A traditional computer does not learn from its mistakes unless it is specifically programmed to do so.

  • Dependence on electricity and maintenance: Computers require a power supply and regular maintenance, and they can be affected by hardware failure, viruses and other faults.

In short, a computer is a fast, accurate and tireless machine, but it remains a tool that depends entirely on human direction.
